# Governments award Edgewing first GCAP contract

By Gareth Jennings |

An artist's rendering of the GCAP future fighter being developed by Italy, Japan, and the UK. The Edgewing industrial consortium received its first governmental contract on 2 April 2026. (Edgewing)

The national governments behind the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) have awarded the first contract to the Edgewing industrial consortium responsible for delivering the trilateral project.

Announced by Edgewing on 2 April, the GBP686 million (USD907 million) award was granted by the GCAP Agency that is part of the GCAP International Government Organisation (GIGO) co-ordinating body for the future fighter programme that comprises Italy, Japan, and the UK.

The award covers key design and engineering activities, and is intended to enable the trilateral partnership to build momentum and accelerate the pace of delivery. “This contract is an important moment for GCAP, as activities previously conducted under three nations' contracts will now be carried out as part of a fully-fledged international programme,” Masami Oka, GCAP Agency Chief Executive, said.

GCAP is a collaborative effort geared at fielding a ‘sixth-generation' combat aircraft for the mid-2030s, with associated unmanned ‘loyal wingmen' and other adjuncts to be developed at a national level.

With the current design phases locked into the three partners, officials have said that there are future opportunities for other countries to join in differing capacities. “All three GCAP nations have highlighted an openness to working with other nations while keeping us on track with the programme schedule and helping us deliver our future military capabilities,” the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in 2025.

While no further countries have yet committed to future participation, interest has been reported from Canada, India, Poland, and Saudi Arabia, among others.

# NATO declares MMU fully operational

By Gareth Jennings |

The MMU has received nine of 12 KC-30M MRTT aircraft, declaring FOC in late March 2026. (NATO Support and Procurement Agency)

NATO has declared its Multinational Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) Unit (MMU) to be fully operational, with nine of the planned 12 Airbus A330 MRTT (KC-30M in alliance service) aircraft now in the Multinational MRTT Fleet (MMF).

Announced on 30 March, the full operating capability (FOC) milestone came three years after initial operating capability (IOC) was declared in 2023.

“FOC is not merely a formal designation; it confirms that the unit can consistently deliver air-to-air refuelling, strategic airlift, and aeromedical evacuation whenever required. This means that the MMU can conduct two deployments simultaneously — a short-term and a long-term deployment — anywhere in the world,” the MMU said.

Operated out of Eindhoven Air Base in the Netherlands, from Cologne-Wahn Air Base in Germany, and at Karup Air Base in Denmark, the MMF sees Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Norway share the use of nine KC-30M aircraft, with a tenth to be delivered in 2027. Two more aircraft were ordered in June 2025 to accommodate Denmark and Sweden joining the MMU, with deliveries due in 2028 and 2029.

# Indian Army charts future of unmanned systems with new technology roadmap

The drone categories include surveillance, loitering munitions, air defence, logistics UAS and special-purpose systems.

With low-cost drones reshaping battlefields, as seen in the United States (US)-Israel war against Iran and the prolonged Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Indian Army on Monday unveiled a roadmap, highlighting a push towards mass and affordable unmanned warfare capabilities.

The 50-page document is titled: ‘*Indian Army’s Technology Roadmap for Unmanned Aerial Systems and Loitering Munitions*’.

It details 30 types of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) and loitering munitions across five categories, translating into nearly 80 variants, a senior army officer said, as cited by news agency *PTI*.

The officer added that the categories include surveillance, loitering munitions, air defence, logistics UAS and special-purpose systems.

Deputy Chief of the Army Staff (Capability Development & Sustenance), Lieutenant General Rahul R Singh, released the document, which aims to provide clear and actionable guidance to industry, academia and research institutions working in the unmanned systems domain.

While addressing the launch event, he cautioned stakeholders about not sharing the document with any unauthorised person due to the risk of it falling into the hands of adversaries.

The move comes amid a global shift in warfare, where inexpensive drones costing just hundreds to a few thousand dollars are being deployed at scale. In the Russia-Ukraine war, both sides have used large volumes of low-cost and loitering drones to destroy high-value targets, including tanks and artillery, changing cost equations on the battlefield. The US has also used the Iranian-modelled LUCAS drone for the first time in the current war.

The roadmap lays out a vision for integrating UAS and loitering munitions across operational roles for the armed forces, providing crucial support to manufacturers to align efforts with the army’s evolving requirements.

The document aims to bridge operational needs and technology development, enabling a structured growth of India’s drone ecosystem while boosting participation from startups, MSMEs and academia in line with the ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ vision.

# Propulsion start-up Beehive receives $30 million USAF contract for low-cost engines

By [Ryan Finnerty](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/ryan-finnerty/) |

**The deal will support flight testing of the 200lb-thrust Frenzy 8 and prototype fabrication on the 100lb-thust Frenzy 6.**

US propulsion start-up Beehive Industries has secured a nearly $30 million contract from the US Air Force to advance testing and development of a new family of low-cost turbojets.

The deal announced on 9 April will fund vehicle integration, flight testing and qualification of the 200 lb-thrust (.89kN) Frenzy 8 engine, which is Beehive’s flagship product. The award also provides funds to support prototype fabrication of the smaller Frenzy 6, which falls into the 100lb-thrust category.

Options for further Frenzy 6 testing, including vehicle integration and a flight demonstration, are also included in the contract.

Beehive describes the deal as a “pivotal step” toward achieving operational readiness and scalable production on the Frenzy line.

“By harnessing additive manufacturing to collapse complex supply chains into scalable, 3D-printed propulsion, we are providing the affordable mass essential to modern deterrence,” says Gordie Follin, chief product officer at Beehive. “This collaboration ensures our warfighters will have the high-volume, mission-ready capabilities they need to maintain a competitive edge in any theater.”

Funding for Frenzy development comes from the USAF’s Small Expendable Turbine programme, which seeks to qualify low-cost, disposable jet engines for uncrewed aircraft and stand-off weapon systems that can be produced at scale.

Magazine depth has [**emerged**](https://www.flightglobal.com/fixed-wing/2026/03/iran-drones-missiles-could-test-rivals-magazine-depth/) as a critical military issue in recent years, particularly when it comes to long-range munitions. Traditional precision-guided weapon systems are expensive and complex, with annual production well below the [**rates of expenditure**](https://www.flightglobal.com/fixed-wing/2026/03/us-air-campaign-shifts-to-gravity-bombs-as-pentagon-officials-downplay-munition-concerns/) observed in recent conflicts, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies **[estimates](https://www.csis.org/analysis/iran-war-cost-estimate-update-113-billion-day-6-165-billion-day-12)** that during the first week of combat in Iran, US forces fired off nearly 1,700 long-range strike and air defence missiles – equivalent to roughly a year’s worth of industrial output.

In the quest to correct that equation, propulsion has emerged as a key limiting factor that both drives cost and restricts the output of long-range munitions. This has [**led to a rush**](https://www.flightglobal.com/engines/2025/09/engine-makers-accelerate-plans-for-new-class-of-small-turbofans-targeting-autonomous-fighters/) of both traditional defence primes like and new start-ups developing small, low-cost jet engines that can power the next generation of cruise missiles and uncrewed aircraft.

Colorado-based Beehive falls into the latter category, with the six-year old company facing off against heavyweights including GE Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Honeywell Aerospace.

In December, the company [**completed**](https://www.flightglobal.com/military-uavs/2025/12/beehive-industries-planning-flight-trials-for-frenzy-turbojet-in-early-2026/) high-altitude lab testing on the Frenzy 8 and said it planned to launch flight testing during the first quarter of 2026. Although Beehive did not meet that goal, the receipt of development funding from the US Air Force means a flight campaign will move forward in the coming months.

Two prototype Frenzy engines were already provided to the air force in 2025 for early evaluation.

If the test campaign goes well, Beehive says it is prepared to launch low-rate production on the Frenzy at facilities in Denver, Cincinnati and Knoxville.

**BAE Systems has successfully conducted a test firing of its APKWS laser-guided rockets from a Eurofighter Typhoon.**

Manufactured by its US subsidiary BAE Systems Inc, the APKWS laser-guidance kit could offer a low-cost solution to counter the threat posed by uncrewed air systems or one-way attack drones.

# First production standard MUAV rolled out in Busan

By [Greg Waldron](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/greg-waldron/) |

**The first mass production example of a new South Korean unmanned air vehicle designed to monitor North Korea has been rolled out, with service entry set for 2027.**

The rollout of the long awaited Korean Airlines Medium Altitude Reconnaissance Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (MUAV) took place at the Korean Air Tech Center in Busan on 8 April, says Seoul’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA).

The uncrewed aircraft, also known as KUS-FS, has been in testing for years and is South Korea’s first strategic UAV. Production of the type **[commenced in Busan in late 2023](https://www.flightglobal.com/military-uavs/2024/12/south-korea-opens-production-centre-for-indigenous-muav-system/)**.

While Korean Air is the prime contractor, LIG Defense & Aerospace and Hanwha Systems are also involved in the programme.

“Although it faced numerous technical challenges during the domestic development process, it overcame them to achieve a high localization rate of 90%,” says DAPA.

“Upon deployment of the [MUAV], it will possess the independent capability to monitor and respond to enemy strategic targets in real time, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, using high-performance cameras and sensors.”

FlightGlobal understands that the initial role for MUAV will be monitoring North Korea using its synthetic aperture radar and electro-optical/infrared sensor. The type will also be deployed by South Korea’s coast guard and navy.

In addition to intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, other roles for the MUAV will include communications relay and electronic warfare.

Korean Air has previously said that the MUAV/KUS-FS system will include two to four UAVs and a ground control system. The aircraft is powered by a 1,200hp (895kW) engine and its dimensions are similar to those of the General Atomics Aeronautical Systems MQ-9 Reaper. The type features a wingspan of 25m (82ft) and a length of 13m.

The MUAV will undergo Republic of Korea Air Force acceptance testing prior to service entry in 2027.

# Indonesia could obtain fifth KF-21 prototype

By [Greg Waldron](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/greg-waldron/) |

**Indonesia could receive a Korea Aerospace Industries KF-21 prototype, although a firm commitment from Jakarta for production examples has yet to emerge.**

As the KF-21 development programme winds down pending service entry in late 2006, Jakarta stands to obtain the fifth prototype in the six-aircraft test fleet, according to South Korean media reports, citing a lawmaker.

The reports come shortly after the rollout of the first production example of the KF-21 on 25 March.

The Indonesian prototype news follows a state visit to South Korea by Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto to Indonesia from 31 March to 2 April. **[Reports prior to the visit](https://www.flightglobal.com/fixed-wing/2026/03/indonesia-to-order-16-kf-21-fighters-during-presidential-visit-yonhap/)** suggested that a firm order for 16 KF-21s would happen during his visit, but this never materialized.

Had the deal happened, it would have marked the first international order for the twin-engined type.

Indonesia, a junior partner in the KF-21, had been due to receive the fifth prototype, a single-seater, earlier in the programme. This never occurred, however, owing to disputes between Jakarta and Seoul about development costs and accusations that Indonesian engineers had stolen programme data.

Ultimately, Jakarta and Seoul rebooted their partnership in June 2025 with Jakarta’s investment in the W8.1 trillion ($5.5 billion) programme reduced to W600 billion from W1.7 trillion previously. Charges against the Indonesian engineers were also dropped.

Even when the relationship faced challenges, however, Jakarta remained hopeful of getting a prototype.

In a 2024 interview with *FlightGlobal*, Indonesian Aerospace president director Gita Amperiawan said that his company **[still hoped to obtain a prototype.](https://www.flightglobal.com/asia-pacific/2024/09/indonesian-aerospace-still-hopeful-of-getting-kf-21-prototype/)**

“I asked the government to have [a prototype],” he said. “The governments are trying to negotiate this, because it’s important.”

# First H145 Jupiter HC2s for Army Air Corps arrive in Brunei

By [Dominic Perry](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/dominic-perry/) |

**British Army aviation units in Brunei have received their first pair of Airbus Helicopters H145 Jupiter HC2s, part of a £148 million ($198 million) 2024 order for six of the light-twins.**

To be operated by 667 Sqn Army Air Corps, the H145s replace now-retired Puma HC2s, that fleet having been withdrawn from service in March 2025.

A total of three [Jupiter HC2s](https://www.flightglobal.com/helicopters/2025/12/uk-takes-latest-jupiter-hc2-pair-ahead-of-brunei-and-cyprus-deployments/) will operate in Brunei in support of the army’s jungle training requirement, performing multiple tasks including medical evacuation, troop transport, firefighting, intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance, and support.

Another three examples of the German-built helicopters, completed at the airframer’s Oxford airport facility in the UK, will be flown by the Royal Air Force’s 84 Sqn in Cyprus.

As in Brunei, they replace Puma HC2s, which were operating in both locations as a stop-gap measure following the earlier retirement of Bell 212/412s.

Both types were due to have been replaced as part of the UK Ministry of Defence’s New Medium Helicopter (NMH) programme, but were ultimately omitted from the requirement which instead focussed on a successor to the RAF’s 23-strong Puma HC2 fleet.

Leonardo Helicopters was last month awarded a [£1 billion contract for NMH](https://www.flightglobal.com/helicopters/2026/03/uk-ministry-of-defence-confirms-aw149-selection-for-nmh-and-adds-more-funding-for-proteus-programme/) covering the acquisition of 23 AW149 super-medium-twins. Delivery is expected over the 2030-2033 period.

# Chilean KC-135 refuels American F-35A fighters en route to FIDAE air show

By [Ryan Finnerty](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/ryan-finnerty/) |

**The US Air Force jets are part of a flight demonstration contingent participating in the biannual FIDAE air show in Santiago, Chile from 7-12 April**

A tanker aircraft from the Chilean air force has for the first time refuelled two American Lockheed Martin F-35A stealth fighters en route to the South American country.

The US Air Force jets are part of a flight demonstration contingent participating in the biannual FIDAE air show in Santiago, Chile from 7-12 April. Photographs released by US Southern Command indicate they are F-35As assigned to the 388th Fighter Wing at Hill AFB in Utah.

That is the parent headquarters for the USAF’s F-35 flight demonstration team, which the Pentagon confirms will be performing at the FIDAE show, in addition to logging the first-ever in-flight refuelling with a Chilean tanker.

The two US stealth fighters were met by a Boeing KC-135E from the Chilean air force during the ferry flight on 5 April. Photos of the encounter indicate the American jets took on fuel offshore before flying south along Chile’s narrow coastline, framed by the towering Andes Mountains.

The Chilean air force confirms the tanking rendezvous took place in international airspace.

“The operation demonstrates interoperability and a high level of readiness of the military aviators,” the service says.

Meanwhile, Washington’s Miami-based headquarters for Latin America says the presence of American assets at FIDAE is a demonstration of the USA’s commitment to the area.

“We are united with our partners to ensure security and stability in the region,” US Southern Command says.

Other US aircraft onsite at FIDAE include a Boeing P-8A anti-submarine warfare jet from the US Navy, a Lockheed Martin C-130J transport and a General Atomics MQ-9A uncrewed aerial vehicle. Photographs indicate one of Chile’s two Boeing E-3 airborne warning and control jets is also at the Santiago show.

“FIDAE allows us to showcase the full range of US airpower while building trusted partnerships alongside Chile and our regional allies,” says Major Gen. David Mineau, commander of US Air Forces Southern.

The air show was opened by Chile’s President Jose Antonio Kast on 7 April.

“We value international collaboration,” Kast said. “Chile wants to bolster relationships with the world stemming from realism, from respect, from defence of its interests and from the values that have made possible free, stable and prosperous societies.”

Four astronauts from the International Space Station also broadcasted a recorded message to help launch the air show.

Demonstration flights planned for FIDAE include an Airbus A400M transport from the Spanish air force and a showcase by both of Chile’s fighter aircraft – the Lockheed Martin F-16 and Northrop F-5E.

# Malaysia operates newly acquired Anka UAVs

By Akhil Kadidal |

A Turkish Aerospace Anka with a Simsek aerial target mounted on the port wing, model displayed at Paris Air Show 2023. (Janes/Sam Wise)

The Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) has test-flown its newly acquired Turkish Aerospace Anka-S unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platform for the first time.

The type's maiden test flight in RMAF service was conducted from Labuan Air Base in the state of Sabah in East Malaysia on 3 April, the air force said on 4 April. The flight confirms the RMAF's induction of the platform, which has been designated as the Anka-THS in Malaysian service.

“The three-hour flight test is part of the preparation before handing over new assets to the RMAF,” the air force added.

Malaysia ordered three Anka-S UAVs in a MYR423.8 million (USD104 million) contract announced in 2023. Malaysia received the three UAVs in January 2026, a Turkish Aerospace spokesperson told *Janes* on 6 April. Ground tests and institutional acceptance procedures have been completed, the spokesperson added.

## Persistent capability

The three UAVs have been deployed with No 11 Squadron at Labuan Air Base, the RMAF said. The service added that the Anka-THS deployment will improve its intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition, and reconnaissance (ISTAR) capabilities in the eastern region and over the South China Sea.

The RMAF also described Labuan as a strategic location for Malaysia, due to its proximity to the South China Sea.

The Anka is a medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) UAV. The platform has a maximum level speed of 140 kt, a maximum take-off weight of 1,700 kg, a radius of action of 135 n miles, and an endurance of 30 hours. The Anka-S configuration includes satellite communications (satcom), secure communications, and a new electro-optic/infrared sensor, according to *Janes* data.

But a shortage of the mini engines is raising concerns about a potential supply crunch for deep-strike drones, more than a dozen arms experts, companies and government officials told Reuters.

"Europe has a massive bottleneck in mini-jet engine production," said Fabian Hoffmann, senior research fellow at the Norwegian Defence University College, adding the sector was also key to helping reduce Europe's reliance on the United States.

A Ukrainian defence industry source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the mini-engine shortage was "probably the main factor limiting the number of missile drones produced," describing it ​as a "big problem for our missile programme".

Maria Popova, COO of the Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry, the biggest association of private weapons manufacturers, agreed there was a bottleneck of turbojets for drones as well as ​the materials needed to build them.

"Supply remains constrained both globally and, more acutely, within Ukraine," she said.

Oleksandr Kamyshin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's arms expert and defence industry adviser, ⁠declined to comment on whether the shortage was having an impact.

## 'STRETCHED TO THE LIMITS'

Deep-strike drones have delivered morale-boosting results for Kyiv at a time when allies are distracted by war in the [Middle East](https://www.reuters.com/world/iran/) and Russia is grinding out ​gains on the ground.

As well as long-range strike drones, mini jet engines power loitering munitions and missile interceptors. With few European manufacturers producing them at scale before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, ramping up output has proved difficult.

Czech-based PBS Group, ​one of the few established producers at the start of the war, has increased production five-fold since 2023 and expects that figure to reach eight-fold by the end of this year as Ukrainian demand surges.

"Our capacities are stretched to the limits," PBS Chief Global Officer Stanislav Lisner told Reuters. "We're investing heavily to expand production," he said, without giving a figure.

PBS has signed an agreement to develop a new engine through a joint venture with Ukraine's Ivchenko-Progress, as part of talks that could include co-production.

PBS's turbojet engines power deep-strike drones ​such as the Palianytsia, which can reach speeds of up to 900 kilometres per hour (559 miles per hour). That compares with about 185 kph for propeller-driven Shahed drones used by Russia, at a cost military experts say is ​far below the $1 million-plus price tag for Western cruise missiles.

They compete with Russia's jet-powered Geran-5 drones, which can fly close to 1,000 km (621 miles) at speeds of up to 600 kph and carry payloads of about 90 kilograms (198 pounds).

## TINY ENGINES, BIG IMPACT

Mini turbojet ‌engines, typically ⁠less than 30 centimetres in diameter, are built from lightweight materials such as titanium alloys, often using 3D-printed components, and generate enough thrust to carry explosive payloads over long distances.

While Russia [sources some engines from China](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/chinese-engines-shipped-cooling-units-power-russian-drones-used-ukraine-2025-07-23/), according to European security officials and documents, Ukraine relies on a small group of European suppliers, including PBS, Germany's JetCat and Netherlands-based Destinus.

"We see increasing demands for these weapons from Ukraine," said Adam Vysocky, head of Czech-based turbojet engine maker ZofiTech, which develops advanced systems including the deep-strike Narwhal drone and Nightray platform.

ZofiTech delivers nearly all the roughly 200 engines it produces each month to Ukraine, and expects demand "to reach thousands in the coming months".

Large aerospace engine manufacturers such as GE Aerospace and Rolls-Royce ​have largely stayed out of the segment, focusing instead on ​more profitable fighter-jet engines.

"There are only a few ⁠companies that are developing these jet engines, and because they are expensive to make the companies will not really start manufacturing them until there's a large government order," said Dominic Surano, director of special projects at defence tech firm Nordic Air Defence.

"That constrains the supply chain."

Some Ukrainian drone makers are working on in-house engine development to reduce dependence on ​suppliers, but production remains limited. Ukrainian engineers are also testing a low-cost pulsejet engine, unveiled in December and known as Hrim-17, aimed at interceptor drones.

"It is peanuts ​compared to what Ukraine needs," said ⁠Estonian defence investor Ragnar Sass.

## DRONE JET ENGINE MARKET 'VERY FAST, VERY HECTIC'

PBS plans to double output at its Czech facility over the next two years as manufacturers expand production lines, hire workers and form partnerships to meet demand, Lisner said. About 25% of PBS deliveries go to Ukraine.

New players are also entering the market.

In February, German drone maker Quantum Systems unveiled a new jet-powered drone developed with Airbus. Nordic Air Defence said it is looking to partner with a stealth startup developing drone motors ⁠from scratch.

Czech defence ​group CSG [(CSG.AS), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/CSG.AS), which went public in January at a valuation of about $35 billion, is expanding into these jet engines after acquiring Serbian manufacturer ​Must Solutions in November.

Pavel Cechal, who leads CSG's jet-engine division, said the company aims to produce about 1,000 turbojet engines in 2026, mainly for deep-strike drones with ranges of 400 to 600 km. About 35% of output is expected to go to Ukraine.

"This market is at the ​moment very fast and very hectic," Cechal said. "Because all the defence companies see a huge potential in that segment."

# YFQ-42A CCA flights paused after California accident

By [Greg Waldron](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/greg-waldron/) |

**A General Atomics Aeronautical Systems (GA-ASI) YFQ-42A collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) has crashed in California.**

The “mishap” occurred after the single-engined CCA took off from a company owned airport, says GA-ASI. Nobody was injured in the incident.

“GA-ASI is assessing the condition of the aircraft and investigating to establish the root cause of the incident,” it says.

“At this early stage, it would be premature to speculate on the circumstances. As with any program, we follow a disciplined investigation process to understand exactly what occurred, and our focus right now is on gathering data and ensuring we learn from this event.”

The YFQ-42A that crashed is among several examples in low-rate initial production for the US Air Force, and GA-ASI says that they fly regularly as part of operational test and evaluation work.

GA-ASI has suspended YFQ-42A operations, but these will resume “when deemed appropriate.”

Says company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley: “Safety is our top priority, for our people and the public. In this case, established procedures and safeguards worked as intended, and there were no injuries. We’re going to take a close look at what happened, gather all the data, and allow the investigation to guide us moving forward.”

The YFQ-42A is one of two uncrewed competitors in the **[USAF’s CCA Increment 1 competition](https://www.flightglobal.com/military-uavs/2026/02/us-air-force-confirms-selection-of-first-autonomous-fighter-coming-by-year-end/)**, which will see 100-150 CCAs obtained by the end of the decade.

The other aircraft involved in the competition is the Anduril Industries YFQ-44A.

# Ascendance advances on Sterna series production with French state backing

By [Dominic Perry](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/dominic-perry/) |

**Hybrid-electric developer Ascendance has secured a €12.2m ($14.2 million) investment over four years from the French government which will enable the start of series production on its Sterna powertrain.**

To be delivered through the France 2030 – Premiere Usine programme, the funding will see Ascendance accelerate the establishment of production capacity for Sterna within its current facilities at Muret L’Herm airfield, to the southwest of Toulouse.

Sterna is being sold to third parties for civil and defence applications and also forms the core of Ascendance’s Atea vertical take-off and landing aircraft.

In a second step, Ascendance plans to create a dedicated manufacturing facility to ramp-up Sterna production, into which it will “progressively integrate assembly of its civil and defence aircraft”, it says.

“This funding enables us to move from prototype to production. It is a decisive step in building a European hybrid-electric sector capable of responding to both decarbonisation and sovereignty imperatives,” says Jean-Christophe Lambert, chief executive, Ascendance.

Ascendance has begun final assembly of its initial Atea prototype and is [targeting a first flight later this year](https://www.flightglobal.com/aerospace/2026/03/ascendance-on-track-for-atea-first-flight-in-2026-as-it-advances-final-assembly-of-vtol-aircraft/).

# United Engine prepares to wrap up certification tests of PD-8

By [David Kaminski-Morrow](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/david-kaminski-morrow/) |

**Russia’s United Engine is preparing to conclude the certification programme for its Aviadvigatel PD-8 powerplant, intended for the Yakovlev SJ-100.**

The company says it has “completed the main set of tests” on the engine, following icing flights in Arkhangelsk which demonstrated “reliable operation in challenging climatic conditions”.

It had previously undertaken three months of icing simulations at the Central Institute of Aviation Motors which included ice build-up on the fan blades, spinner and low-pressure compressor in water-saturated air.

“A calibrated sprayer was used to wet the air flow entering the engine inlet,” says United Engine.

“The tests were conducted to evaluate engine stability and controllability in icing conditions, as well as the strength of structural components during the shedding of accumulated ice.”

Over the course of the SJ-100 flight-test programme in Arkhangelsk during March, the PD-8 was subjected to severe icing with the formation of an 8-10mm crust.

“These conditions simultaneously test several important parameters,” says United Engine, among them dynamic gaseous stability at the air intake, the effectiveness of anti-ice systems, and the aircraft’s overall safe operation.

It says the flights confirmed the predicted characteristics across the entire altitude range, and the results of rig testing.

“Despite the harsh operating conditions of ice build-up, the engine continued to operate normally and maintained thrust,” states United Engine deputy sales director Fyodor Mironov.

The PD-8 engine has previously completed a 150h session simulating long-term operation, and passed other demanding tests for bird-strike resilience, fan-blade fracture, and water ingestion.

United Engine adds that the powerplant, operating at its 8t (78kN) thrust level, has confirmed its performance in crosswind and acoustic tests. The PD-8 is intended not only for the SJ-100 but also the amphibious Beriev Be-200 firefighter.

# Clean Aviation HERFUSE project details weight-loss plan for future turboprop

By [Dominic Perry](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/dominic-perry/) |

**A project led by Leonardo’s aerostructures unit will later this year begin tests on a series of new composite fuselage and empennage components that could contribute significant weight-saving to a future regional turboprop.**

Alongside building the physical demonstrators, [the HERFUSE project](https://herfuse.eu/) – part funded through the EU’s [Clean Aviation initiative](https://www.clean-aviation.eu/) – continues to analyse the integration requirements of alternative energy sources into the fuselages of two different future aircraft architectures.

Running until December 2026, with testing over the June-September period, HERFUSE is focused in the near-term on what Clean Aviation calls the [Ultra Efficient Regional Aircraft (UERA) concept](https://www.flightglobal.com/engines/2025/11/clean-aviation-lays-out-goals-for-next-project-call-as-rise-engine-waits-for-take-off-clearance/) – a hybrid-electric design with four-abreast seating seen as a potential new member of the ATR family from 2035 onwards.

But looking further ahead, a second aircraft concept is also being considered, featuring a five-abreast cabin and powered by hydrogen fuel cells.

While several technologies and components being developed through HERFUSE are only likely to be for the longer term, others have been designed with a shorter route to exploitation in mind.

By using new manufacturing methods and materials, HERFUSE is creating lighter versions of current components used on the reference aircraft, the ATR 72-600, that could be introduced as like-for-like replacements, explains Fabrizio Leone, research and development project manager at Leonardo.

These include a composite window frame produced using automated fibre-patch placement and an “innovative” composite floor beam. In both cases, they would replace existing metallic parts, saving weight and shaving production time through the introduction of automated processes, says Leone.

For the floor beam alone, the weight saving is estimated about 10% versus the metallic component, he says: “The evaluation of the exact figure is still in progress, but we are confident we will get there.”

Assembly of a full-scale vertical empennage torque box demonstrator has also commenced, featuring a blend of riveted and bonded composite construction.

Although traditional fasteners are still present, the secondary bonding of pre-cured parts – a technique common in other industries such as automotive – should allow a significant number of rivets to be removed, reducing weight compared to the same structural component on the ATR 72.

On top of technology maturation, the HERFUSE team is also working with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to develop a certification roadmap, paving the way for the introduction of the new parts on current aircraft.

“We are discussing the regulation gaps and the potential means of compliance on this technology” using current standards as the starting point, says Leone.

“Of course, it will require the step from research to industrialisation of the process, but in this phase one project we are laying the foundations.”

Meanwhile, the HERFUSE team is also working with other projects within Clean Aviation’s regional aircraft pillar to ensure the technologies they are developing can be integrated within its design for the UERA fuselage.

These include the high-voltage electrical distribution system developed through the [Collins Aerospace-led project HECATE](https://www.flightglobal.com/engines/2023/02/collins-led-hecate-project-looks-to-harness-magic-as-part-of-electrification-push/), and the next-generation thermal management system designed by TheMa4HERA, a project co-ordinated by [Honeywell Aerospac](https://www.flightglobal.com/europe/2025/10/czech-mates-why-brno-base-is-key-to-honeywells-international-ambitions/)e.

For the UERA concept, HERFUSE has also conducted trade studies to identify the most suitable area of the aircraft to host the battery pack plus its thermal management system – assessing the impact on passenger numbers and space for luggage.

In addition to understanding the requirements of the architectures they are presented with, Leone says the HERFUSE team is also “considering ergonomic constraints from potential operations in the airport” – turnaround or charging times and, in future, how the battery packs could be swapped out.

Similarly, the project has analysed the most suitable location for the hydrogen fuel tanks of the future fuel cell-powered variant and for the fuel cells themselves.

While still to be confirmed, the underfloor area of the fuselage is thought the most likely location for the battery packs, while the hydrogen fuel tank would be in the rear fuselage, behind the aft pressure bulkhead.

A final task for the project is to also complete the preliminary design review for the hybrid-electric flying testbed ATR is developing under a [second-phase Clean Aviation project](https://www.flightglobal.com/airframers/2025/09/atr-hybrid-electric-aircraft-among-programmes-sharing-latest-clean-aviation-funding/) called DEMETRA. Flight tests are due to take place towards the end of the decade.

The results from the ongoing technology development and design activities will support ATR’s assessment about the most appropriate evolution of the successful regional aircraft family, spanning from incremental evolution of existing aircraft to the development of an entirely new one.

ATR is a joint venture between Airbus and Leonardo.

# Special Report: US companies agree to invest in increased production capacity for THAAD, PrSM

By Meredith Roaten & Carlo Munoz & Jeremiah Cushman |

THAAD systems have been deployed to the CENTCOM area of responsibility regularly in recent years. (378th Air Expeditionary Wing)

The US Department of Defense (DoD) has signed multiple framework agreements with four major defence contractors to increase production of missiles and their components for Operation ‘Epic Fury' in Iran.

The agreements will invest in production facilities for Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Terminal High Altitude Air Defense (THAAD) seekers, Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) seekers, and other electronic components, according to multiple recent statements. The government cannot buy more munitions without approval from lawmakers.

A DoD spokesperson declined to answer additional questions from *Janes.*

Strikes in Iran as well as defences against Iranian cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past month have taken a toll on US missile stores. The agreements come after defence executives were invited to the White House in early March to discuss expended weapons. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and other officials have said that munitions stockpiles are sufficient to support the US military objectives during the operation.

Each agreement is “a core component of the department's broader effort to place the acquisition system on a ‘wartime footing', prioritizing speed and flexibility to outpace adversaries”, according to a 1 April DoD statement.

## THAAD

Both THAAD and Patriot interceptors have been used to defend US installations and ground assets in the Middle East in recent weeks, according to DoD statements.

Iran's ability to launch missiles at US targets is trending downward, Joint Chief of Staff General Dan Caine told reporters on 31 March. But “they are still shooting”, he said.

# KNDS France completes acquisition of Texelis Defense as latter accelerates activities

By Nicholas Fiorenza |

KNDS Mobility plans to launch SCATA's Mk1 4x4 vehicle at Eurosatory 2026. (SCATA)

KNDS France announced on 2 April 2026 that it had completed its acquisition of Texelis Defense, which has become KNDS Mobility.

KNDS France said in a press release that the acquisition would support its growth strategy: to increase its industrial capabilities, control key technologies, and ramp up production.

The company expects the acquisition to reduce supply chain dependencies and to consolidate capabilities such as drivetrains and vehicle mobility solutions across 4x4, 6x6, 8x8, and tracked classes. KNDS expects its offer across mobility, protection, observation, attack, and mission systems to improve as a result, accelerating development cycles and improving end-to-end control of land products. It sees potential future gains in technological areas such as energy optimisation and platform autonomy, with plans to develop its Track Electrified Drivetrain (TED) designed for manned and unmanned tracked vehicles.

KNDS France plans to leverage and strengthen existing technological and commercial partnerships, particularly for the Serval (Véhicule Blindé Multi-Rôle Léger: VBMR-L) 4x4 light multirole armoured vehicle programme, with KNDS Mobility providing the mobility system and KNDS France manufacturing and assembling the integrated vehicle and supplying associated equipment.

On 23 March, 10 days before the completion of the acquisition, then Texelis Defense said in a press release that it expected to benefit from the accelerated development of the Serval programme and the first export contracts for the vehicle, as well as from accelerated progress with the Celeris vehicle. # Aura secures new finance and targets late 2027 for ERA first flight

By [Murdo Morrison](https://www.flightglobal.com/author/murdo-morrison/) |

**A freshly refinanced Aura Aero insists its hybrid-electric ERA will take to the skies next year – albeit a few months after the “early 2027” date the Toulouse-based start-up was targeting this time last year. Speaking to FlightGlobal, chief executive Jeremy Caussade declares the business is “pretty much on track deliver the first prototype to flight test by mid-2027”.**

It follows the company’s announcement in early March of French private aviation operator Pan Europeenne Air Service (PEAS) as launch customer for the 19-seat, in-development aircraft. The size of the order was not disclosed, but PEAS had previously said it intends to buy four examples. Although Aura claims to have 700 letters of intent from 16 prospective customers, this is its first declared firm order.

On 8 April, the company announced it had completed a new €50 million ($58 million) funding round, which, together with €120 million in subsidies and €170 million funding from the State of Florida for a new stateside factory in Daytona Beach, takes its available funding to €340 million, according to Caussade.

Aura is also preparing for construction later this year of an assembly plant at its Francazal airport base to replace its existing factory. At the same time, it is stepping up production of its two-seat Integral training and aerobatic aircraft, which it will offer alongside the ERA (or Electric Regional Aircraft).

Design has been fixed on the ERA prototype taking shape at Aura’s current factory in a Second World War-era one-time military hangar at Francazal. “This year is about transforming the frozen design into a workable prototype,” says Caussade, who adds that Aura will build three or four flight test examples, as well as two others for fatigue and other ground testing.

Aura has an end-of-decade target to achieve service entry for the hybrid commuter and VIP airliner – which is powered by eight Safran ENGINeUS electric motors and two conventionally fueled turbo generators. It could be the first clean sheet contender in decades in a segment once dominated by the Beechcraft 1900, Dornier 228, Fairchild Metroliner and De Havilland Twin Otter.

Meanwhile, Aura aims to deliver 15 examples of its two-seat aerobatic trainer this year after shipping three Integral Rs in 2025 – the R is the first of three variants. Around September, Caussade hopes to shift from rate one to rate two a month, with production boosted by two examples of the sportier S version once that receives its expected certification in the final quarter.

Thus far, the Lycoming AEIO-390-powered Integral R has been approved only by European regulators, but Caussade anticipates Federal Aviation Administration certification by the fourth quarter. In July last year, Aura announced that Plymouth, Massachusetts-based training school Michael Goulian Aviation would be the first US customer for the aircraft, after it placed an order for two examples.

The third, and arguably most technically challenging, E or electrical variant is taking longer. Aura has been flying a single prototype of the ENGINeUS-powered aircraft since December 2024 and plans to have three examples in the air by the end of the year. However, it does not expect European regulatory approval until late 2027 or early 2028.

That timetable would likely make the Integral E the second purely electric aircraft to be certificated. However, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency CS-23-category trainer is a larger and more sophisticated product than the Velis Electro from Textron-owned Pipistrel, classified as a light sport aircraft when it was approved in 2020.

Caussade says “feedback has been great” from the flight test programme but that Aero will take a cautious approach to certification when it comes to the E. “Although we’ve had zero problems so far, we need to have 500 to 1,000 flight hours before we start deliveries,” he says. “We don’t want to put it on the market too early until we have ironed out any reliability issues.”

In addition, the company intends to unveil a prototype unmanned air vehicle at this June’s Eurosatory defence exhibition in Paris for a possible French or wider European requirement for a domestically built medium-range, long-endurance platform. It aims to fly the aircraft this year from an undisclosed location in France with a targeted certification date of late 2028.

Aura last year announced its intention to enter the defence market by developing a drone to compete with the likes of the US-manufactured General Atomics MQ-9 Reaper as well as products made by Turkish and Israeli companies in use by European militaries. “There is a need more than ever for a European drone,” says Caussade.

The company has been developing the ERA and manufacturing its existing two-seat Integral aircraft at its original facility at Francazal and in October last year opened a stopgap maintenance and assembly hangar on the Embry Riddle Aeronautical University campus in Florida to prepare the ground for US certification of both aircraft.

With a public consultation winding up in February and most planning approvals in place, Caussade says Aura is now on final approach to getting spades in the ground for its new Francazal factory. A detailed survey on the site has begun and he expects construction to begin in the second half of the year, with completion by the end of 2028 in time for production the following year.

The planned new US plant in Daytona Beach will initially carry out final assembly, outfitting and painting of aircraft for the North American market before moving into detailed parts machining after about five years. Situated near the existing Embry Riddle facility, construction there will focus on the ERA.

While Francazal will remain the heart of the Integral and ERA programmes, Caussade says it was vital to establish a US footprint, not just for efficiency and to be closer to customers but to solidify Aura’s relationship with the FAA.

He expects Daytona Beach to eventually assemble more units than France but says that once Aura establishes a two-year backlog – it is currently just short of 18 months – the company will have enough “visibility” to smartly allocate production between the two sites at several months’ notice.

To avoid diverting precious cash to capital expenditure, Aura plans to work with a property developer to build and rent back the 20,000sq m (215,000sq ft) Francazal factory, which will eventually be capable of producing 150 aircraft a year – roughly 100 ERAs and 50 Integrals. It will take a similar approach in the USA.

A canny approach to its finances has been a mainstay of the way Aura has done business since former Airbus executive Caussade set up the company with two colleagues in 2018. It rents its hangar at Francazal, a rather forlorn former military base southwest of the city with weeds sprouting from former taxiways and buildings in need of a lick of paint, but one that puts it in the middle of one of the largest aerospace supply chains and talent pools in Europe.

Crucially, unlike most of its fellow advanced air mobility start-ups which have opted to certificate disruptive clean sheet technology in an all-new segment, Aura will finance much of its early activities with revenue from the Integral programme, a much more conventional aircraft to certificate than the ERA, and with a ready market of flight schools.

Before the 8 April announcement, the company had raised around €134 million in non-equity finance, while French energy company EDF had taken equity through its innovation fund. Last year, it announced it was increasing its stake in Aura to €2 million in a bid to “accelerate aviation decarbonisation”.

While PEAS is Aura’s only confirmed customer so far, a string of operators has signed tentative agreements for the aircraft. Among the latest to sign a tentative agreement last year were Greek wet-lease specialist Marathon, which wants to take up to 40 examples, and Kenyan regional operator Safarilink. They join the likes of Maltese private aviation firm Elit’Avia, regional cargo airline Alpine Air Express and US charter outfit JetSuiteX.

Caussade expects VIP configurations to make up a healthy chunk of ERA orders, with the aircraft, he says, offering a wider and more comfortable cabin and lower running costs than competitors such as the Pilatus PC-12 and Piper M700 single-engine turboprops.

However, he expects the need to replace “thousands” of previous-generation 19-seat commuter aircraft to represent the bulk of demand. “On the commercial side, the need for this plane is clearly there,” he says. “It is cost-efficient, safe, available and, importantly, quiet. This is especially important in Europe where there is such a focus on CO2 emissions and noise. This aircraft could be a way for a local airport close to a densely populated area to survive.”

April 6 (Reuters) - Fire Point, maker of Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missile, is in talks with European companies to launch a new air defence system by next year, a senior executive told Reuters, creating a low-cost alternative to the increasingly hard-to-get ​Patriot system.

With governments seeking to defend their skies as the [wars in Ukraine](https://www.reuters.com/world/ukraine-russia-war/) and [Iran](https://www.reuters.com/world/iran/) sow global instability, Fire Point's co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilierman said it aimed to slash the cost of intercepting ‌a ballistic missile to below $1 million.

Shtilierman also said Fire Point was awaiting government approval for an investment by a Middle Eastern conglomerate that valued the company at $2.5 billion and would open the door to new business opportunities, including low-orbit satellite launches.

Years of know-how gained on the battlefield fighting Russian forces have made Ukraine a leading innovator in low-cost defence tech. With the outbreak of war in the Gulf, [Kyiv has leveraged](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/ukraines-drone-masters-eye-iran-war-kickstart-export-ambitions-2026-03-30/) that expertise to sign security agreements with governments across the region.

Many Ukrainian defence firms are now seeking to export their excess capacity and cash ​in on a global boom in military spending. While the government recently loosened wartime export restrictions, each proposed deal is still subject to stringent checks and state approval.

## DEVELOPING AN ALTERNATIVE TO THE PATRIOT SYSTEM

Ukraine and many ​other Western-allied nations rely heavily on the U.S.-made Patriot system to stop ballistic missiles.

But Patriot missiles are in [increasingly short supply](https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/iran-conflict-may-divert-us-weapons-ukraine-2026-03-04/) amid extensive deployment in the Gulf against Iranian attacks. ⁠And Europe's only anti-ballistic system, the Italo-French SAMP/T, is produced in relatively small numbers.

To bring down a ballistic projectile, the Patriot system - manufactured by Raytheon and Lockheed Martin [(LMT.N), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/LMT.N) - often requires two or three air defence missiles, each costing several million ​dollars, Shtilierman said.

"If we can decrease it to less than $1 million, it will be ... a game changer in air defence solutions," he said in an interview. "We plan to intercept the first ballistic missile at the end of 2027."

Shtilierman declined to ​name the European companies involved in the discussions to develop the new system but said Fire Point is "deeply interested" in collaboration on radar, missile target-seeking and communications systems - areas where it lacks expertise.

European companies including Weibel, Hensoldt [(HAGG.DE), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/HAGG.DE), SAAB [(SAABb.ST), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/SAABb.ST) and Thales [(TCFP.PA), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/TCFP.PA) have good radar solutions, he noted.

Founded after Moscow's 2022 invasion, Fire Point is Ukraine's biggest maker of the long-range drones used in the majority of strikes deep inside Russia.

In recent months, its FP5 long-range cruise missile - commonly known as the Flamingo - has also been used to hit Russian military facilities and arms ​factories, including a ballistic missile plant nearly [1,400 km (870 miles) inside Russian territory](https://www.reuters.com/world/governor-udmurtia-southern-russia-says-ukrainian-drones-damaged-site-2026-02-20/).

Shtilierman said Fire Point was now in the final stages of developing two supersonic ballistic missiles.

The smaller FP-7 missile, with a range of around 300 km, will have its ​first military deployment "in the close future", he said, describing it as similar to Lockheed Martin's [ATACMS short-range ballistic system](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/ukraine-hits-targets-russia-with-atacms-military-says-2025-11-18/).

The larger FP-9, capable of carrying an 800 kg warhead up to 850 km, is about to enter testing and would place Moscow within range of Ukraine's ‌ballistic arsenal, he ⁠added.

Shtilierman said strikes on Moscow, which is ringed by some of the world's most formidable air defences, would cause a "mass shift in the Russian mind and the mind of top guys in Russia."

Russia's defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

Fabian Hoffmann, a missile expert and senior researcher at the Norwegian Defence University College, said that, while Russia has experience in successfully downing ATACMS, more widespread use of ballistic missiles could stretch Russian air defences, already degraded by Ukrainian strikes.

And while Fire Point's 2027 target for launching a low-cost air defence system was "ambitious", he said that, beyond Ukraine's own military needs, there would be strong demand from governments even if its kill rates per missile were less effective than the Patriot's.

## UAE ​INVESTMENT COULD START SATELLITE VENTURE

Ukraine's anti-monopoly authority has until around ​October to decide on the proposed $760-million acquisition of ⁠a 30% stake in Fire Point by the Middle Eastern investor, Shtilierman said.

Ukrainian media have identified the suitor as Emirati defence firm [Edge Group, opens new tab](https://forbes.ua/innovations/amku-lishe-odin-z-elementiv-komitet-povernuv-zayavku-vid-arabskogo-fondu-edge-na-kupivlyu-chastki-ukrainskoi-fire-point-shcho-galmue-ugodu-na-25-mlrd-16032026-37116). Edge Group and Ukraine's anti-monopoly authorities did not respond to a request for comment.

The investment would be the first step in a project to build a space launch terminal in the UAE, with the aim of eventually establishing ​a constellation of low-orbit European satellites. Shtilierman said the country's location next to the Indian Ocean and geographical conditions were favourable for space launches.

"We built a carbon winding ​machine, which allows us to wind ⁠a big solid rocket booster for satellite delivery," he said, noting the project remained at the conceptual stage although there were already agreements "with a couple of Western companies".

Regardless of whether the UAE deal proceeds, Shtilierman said Fire Point would not take on further investors until after it had demonstrated success with its missile defence system, which will use the company's FP7 missile. .

Fire Point has, meanwhile, received interest from Gulf states for purchases of its existing drone products and is awaiting approval from Ukraine's government to begin ⁠exports. Shtilierman said ​the company has monthly capacity to export up to 2,500 long-range drones.

Exporting the Flamingo missile, however, is much more difficult due to regulatory barriers, ​he said.

Fire Point says it makes hundreds of long-range strike drones a day, each costing about 50,000 euros ($57,775) to produce, and three Flamingo missiles, at a cost of about 600,000 euros apiece. He acknowledged some "bottleneck" issues with the Flamingo, including with engine production.

Fire Point will increase production of the ​Flamingo when a new, in-house engine goes into mass production in October and a rocket fuel plant in Denmark comes online later this year, he said. The plant is awaiting two final approvals from Danish authorities.
